text.p: Women vaccinated against rubella -- a common precaution against birth defects -- do not appear to run a higher risk of developing arthritis or other joint diseases, researchers said on Tuesday.
The report from the Northern California Kaiser Permanente Vaccine Study Center in Oakland was based on a look at more than 4,000 women, some of whom had not been vaccinated against the disease.
The researchers said they found no increased risk of arthritis, lupus, chronic fatigue syndrome, fibromyalgia and a number of other conditions among those who had been vaccinated.

Some previous studies had suggested there might be a link between rubella vaccinations and chronic joint diseases. But the study said the new findings "support the continued vaccination of rubella-susceptible women of childbearing age ..."

Rubella, sometimes called German measles, can cause severe birth defects if women develop the disease in the early stages of pregnancy. U.S. public health guidelines recommend that everyone 12 months of age and older with no immunity to rubella be vaccinated.
Women who give birth and are found to lack immunity should be vaccinated before discharge from the hospital to ward off potential problems in future pregnancies, the guidelines suggest.
The study was published in this week's Journal of the American Medical Association.
